name: Anecdotal Fallacy
description: A vivid personal story can outweigh broader statistical evidence, leading people to generalize from one memorable case instead of the larger pattern. Concrete anecdotes feel more diagnostic than pallid summaries.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to research synthesis, support triage, and roadmap prioritization: one loud customer story or memorable interview clip can dominate a much larger body of analytics, survey data, or mixed-method evidence.
prevalence_note: Widely used in critical-thinking, analytics, and research-ops conversations whenever vivid user stories start overruling the dataset.

findings.description: In course-choice decisions, abstract statistical summaries had little impact whereas brief concrete comments from other students had substantial impact, showing that vivid person-level evidence can outweigh broader numerical base-rate information.
findings.source_title: The Differential Impact of Abstract vs. Concrete Information on Decisions

applications.title: Nielsen warns against drawing sweeping lessons from whichever side wins Amazon vs. Barnes & Noble
applications.description: Nielsen Norman Group's 'Fallacy of Atypical Web Examples' article, written by Jakob Nielsen, uses the well-publicized rivalry between Amazon.com and Barnes & Noble as an example of how observers draw a single, sweeping causal lesson ('brick-based companies are too slow to compete online' or, conversely, 'an established brand and marketing muscle is what counts') from whichever company appears to be winning. Nielsen's more valid analysis: the actual outcome depends on many simultaneous factors (discount depth, server speed, uptime, UI quality, inbound links), and much of Amazon's own advantage was itself an atypical amount of free press coverage as an early internet-commerce success story -- a concrete illustration of how a single highly-publicized rivalry gets overgeneralized into a general business rule.
applications.ethical_note: A strategic-reasoning error a design/business team can make against itself, with no user-facing persuasive or manipulative dimension.

applications.title: Nielsen warns against generalizing 'advertising works' from Yahoo!'s atypical success
applications.description: Nielsen Norman Group's 'Fallacy of Atypical Web Examples' article, written by Jakob Nielsen, names Yahoo!'s profitability from web advertising as a real, widely-cited example that teams wrongly generalize into 'advertising is a viable revenue model for the majority of websites.' Nielsen's more valid analysis: only the top fraction of a percent of sites by traffic can make enough from pure ad impressions, so a strategy team basing its own revenue-model decision on Yahoo!'s highly-publicized, atypical case -- rather than on the actual traffic and audience realities of its own site -- is a real, concrete illustration of the anecdotal fallacy applied to product/business strategy, not just to individual customer stories.
applications.ethical_note: A strategic-reasoning error a design/business team can make against itself, with no user-facing persuasive or manipulative dimension.
